title: Valerian
subtitle: The strong-smelling sleep root of western herbal tradition
excerpt: Valerian root is the western kitchen's primary sleep herb: a strongly aromatic preparation taken before bed for difficulty falling asleep. It carries significant cautions around sedative medicines, alcohol, and driving. Limited clinical-trial evidence supports the traditional use for sleep onset.

glossaryTerms.definition: An action that promotes sleep and reduces nervous activity. Unlike gentle nervine herbs, sedative herbs carry real cautions around combining with other sedative medicines or alcohol.
The primary active constituent of valerian root, associated with the herb's sedative and antispasmodic properties.

content.text: Valerian in the home kitchen is the strongly aromatic root preparation taken before bed. It comes as a cup of earthy-smelling tea or as an alcohol extract in a small glass of water. Western herbal tradition has used it for sleep for at least a thousand years: mainly for difficulty falling asleep when the obstacle is a restless, overactive mind. Limited trial evidence supports the traditional use for sleep onset. An alcohol extract in 40% spirit stores for two years.
Precautions
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.

Sedative medicines: valerian potentiates (adds to the effect of) benzodiazepines such as diazepam or lorazepam, barbiturates, sleeping tablets, antihistamines with a sedative effect, and any other medicine that acts on the central nervous system to cause drowsiness. Do not combine. If you are on any of these medicines and are considering valerian, speak to your prescriber first.
Alcohol: the same caution applies to alcohol. Valerian and alcohol together produce a stronger sedative effect than either alone. Do not take valerian on an evening when you are drinking.

Driving and operating machinery: if it is your first time using valerian, take it only at bedtime and do not drive or operate machinery the following morning until you know how it affects you. Some readers experience residual drowsiness the next day, particularly at higher doses.
Pregnancy: consult a herbalist or your midwife before using valerian in pregnancy. The herb has not been adequately studied in pregnancy, and its sedative action puts it in the cautious column.
Botanical

Valeriana officinalis, family Caprifoliaceae. Valerian is a tall herbaceous perennial with clusters of small pale-pink flowers in midsummer. It grows in damp meadows and hedgerows across Europe and temperate Asia. The parts used are the root and rhizome, harvested in autumn of the second year when the plant is well established. The fresh root has little smell; it develops the characteristic strong, earthy, slightly unpleasant odour on drying, from the breakdown of compounds in the volatile fraction. Cats are famously attracted to valerian root and will chew through a dried preparation given the chance.
active compounds and actions

The main active compound is valerenic acid, linked to the sedating action through GABA receptors. Valepotriates were once considered the main actives but break down quickly on storage. They are now seen as secondary. The volatile oil gives valerian its distinctive smell and is thought to contribute to the overall effect. Distinct from the gentler calming herbs such as chamomile or lemon balm.
Traditional uses

Western herbal and folk European traditions have used valerian root as a sleep herb and a nerve herb for at least a thousand years. The primary application is sleep-onset difficulty: the reader who lies awake with a busy mind rather than one whose sleep is disturbed by pain or other physical causes. Valerian is also long used for nervous tension, muscle spasm (especially gut spasm). And anxiety with a physical edge, where the restlessness is felt in the body as well as the mind.

Valerian has a long record in British folk medicine for nervous distress and sleep problems. Its current use is more specific. The sleep application has the most modern evidence. Trial evidence supports the traditional use for reducing the time to fall asleep, mainly in mild to moderate sleep difficulty.
Preparations

A simmered preparation is the most effective way to prepare dried valerian root, which is woody and does not give up its active compounds well in a simple steep. Simmer one teaspoon of dried root in a cup of water, covered, for fifteen minutes, then strain. The taste is bitter and earthy; honey improves it. Drink thirty to forty minutes before bed.

Valerian alcohol extract in 40% spirit (1 part dried root to 5 parts spirit, macerated for four to six weeks) provides a more concentrated and reliable preparation. The standard dose from a alcohol extract is 1 to 3 ml in a small amount of water, taken thirty minutes before bed. alcohol extract stores for two years in a dark glass bottle away from light.

Valerian is often combined with other calming herbs: hops, passionflower, or lemon balm. The combinations extend the traditional sleep formula to include both the deeper sedative root and the gentler nerve-calming leaves. Do not combine with prescription sedative or hypnotic medicines.
Cautions and cautions
Sedative medicines: valerian adds to the effect of all sedating medicines. Do not combine it with sleeping tablets or benzodiazepines. The combined effect can be unpredictable.
Alcohol: alcohol is a CNS depressant and the same potentiation applies. Do not take valerian on a night when you are drinking alcohol.
Driving: some readers feel drowsy the next morning, mainly at higher doses. Take valerian only at bedtime on your first use. Check how you feel the following morning before driving.
Pregnancy: valerian has not been studied enough in pregnancy. Consult a herbalist or your midwife before using it.
Children under twelve: doses for children are not half an adult dose. Consult a herbalist who specialises in children's herbal medicine before using valerian in children.
